paras: The Yorktown mob pursuit was the chase of an unnamed Black man by a mob of twenty-five men at Yorktown, Indiana, six miles west of Muncie, reported in a dispatch dated November 2, 1903. The man escaped by jumping into the river and swimming across, and no one was reported hurt. The report was notable for stating the motive plainly: "Colored men are unpopular in the village Yorktown."

According to the Muncie dispatch, Black men were unwelcome in the village, and the man drew attention when he was "seen prowling around the place in a suspicious manner." The dispatch did not accuse him of any crime, and the description of his conduct is the pursuers' side of the story.

A mob of twenty-five of the village's "best citizens," as the dispatch put it, set out after him. He ignored their order to halt and hurried away with the mob close behind. He finally got away by jumping into the river and swimming to the other side. The report gives neither his name nor the names of any of the pursuers.
No report of arrests, of any official action or of the man's later fate appears in the coverage.

The only report found ran in the Plymouth Tribune of November 5, 1903, as a short item in a page-eight column of Indiana news under the headline "Drove a Negro Into the River." It shared the column with items on a tramp camp at Frankfort, an attempted safe robbery at Greencastle and a treasurer's shortage at Vincennes. The dispatch named the village's hostility to Black men as the setting, repeated the "prowling" claim without comment, and put "best citizens" in quotation marks, a touch that reads as ironic.
No account in the Black press was found, and no other white paper carrying the dispatch turned up.

accounts.label: Muncie dispatch
accounts.gist: Colored men were unpopular at Yorktown; when a Black man was seen prowling suspiciously, twenty-five 'best citizens' chased him, and he escaped across the river.

framing.detail: The headline 'Drove a Negro Into the River' and the line that 'colored men are unpopular' name the racial motive plainly, the 'prowling' claim is passed on as fact, and the quotation marks around 'best citizens' read as ironic.
